content: Alkaline tide is a physiological phenomenon that occurs after the consumption of a meal. It is characterized by a temporary increase in the pH of the blood due to the release of stomach acid into the stomach. This process is a normal function of the body. The mechanism behind alkaline tide involves an increase in carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration within the active stomach wall. This CO2 is converted into bicarbonate (HCO3-) by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase. The production of bicarbonate leads to a rise in blood pH. In children, this shift in pH can sometimes result in a condition referred to as alkaline tide bicarbonate, where bicarbonate enters the bloodstream. During the secretion of hydrochloric acid (HCl) in the stomach, the gastric parietal cells extract chloride (Cl-) ions, CO2, water (H2O), and sodium (Na+) cations from the blood plasma. These components are used to form HCl. After the formation of HCl, bicarbonate is released back into the plasma to maintain the electrical balance of the plasma, compensating for the extraction of Clions. Since bicarbonate is an alkaline substance, the venous blood leaving the stomach becomes more alkaline compared to the arterial blood that is delivered to the stomach. This difference in alkalinity is a direct result of the bicarbonate being returned to the bloodstream.
